text: Abstention from injuring (creatures), veracity, abstention from unlawfully appropriating (the goods of others), purity, and control of the organs, Manu has declared to be the summary of the law for the four castes.
context_note: Ahimsa heads Manu's own summary of dharma binding on everyone regardless of caste — the baseline beneath all role-specific duties.

text: He who thinks it to be the killer and he who thinks it to be killed, both know nothing. It kills not, is not killed.
context_note: Krishna's metaphysical consolation to Arjuna: the self is beyond slaying. The tradition reads this as reframing death, never as license — the duty context of the warrior is essential.

text: One may slay without hesitation an assassin who approaches (with murderous intent), whether (he be one's) teacher, a child or an aged man, or a Brahmana deeply versed in the Vedas.
context_note: The atatayin (violent aggressor) rule: against an actual assassin, defense is permitted regardless of the attacker's status — the dharmashastra's explicit self-defense provision.

text: Having regard to your own duty also, you ought not to falter, for there is nothing better for a Kshatriya than a righteous battle.
context_note: Arjuna's duty as a warrior in a righteous cause is the Gita's frame: war can be dharma for the one whose station it is — 'righteous' is load-bearing.

text: Let him (heartily) strive to conquer his foes by conciliation, by (well-applied) gifts, and by creating dissension, used either separately or conjointly, never by fighting, (if it can be avoided).
context_note: Manu's statecraft ranks war last: conciliation, gifts, and diplomacy first — battle only when unavoidable. A brake on any easy reading of kshatriya duty.

text: Libations of water shall not be offered to those who (neglect the prescribed rites and may be said to) have been born in vain, to those born in consequence of an illegal mixture of the castes, to those who are ascetics (of heretical sects), and to those who have committed suicide;
context_note: Denial of funeral libations marks suicide from despair as condemned; the dharma literature treats self-killing as a grave transgression of one's remaining duties.

text: Or let him walk, fully determined and going straight on, in a north-easterly direction, subsisting on water and air, until his body sinks to rest.
context_note: The 'great departure' (mahaprasthana) permitted to the renunciant at life's end — a ritualized, duty-completed walking-out sharply distinguished from suicide in despair.

text: Meat can never be obtained without injury to living creatures, and injury to sentient beings is detrimental to (the attainment of) heavenly bliss; let him therefore shun (the use of) meat.
context_note: The vegetarian argument stated as causation: meat entails harm, harm impedes the highest ends. This sits in a chapter that also records older sacrificial permissions.

text: There is no sin in eating meat, in (drinking) spirituous liquor, and in carnal intercourse, for that is the natural way of created beings, but abstention brings great rewards.
context_note: Manu's own counter-verse: the natural appetites are not sin, yet abstention is higher. The tradition's layered view — permission below, renunciation above — in one line.

text: Stipulated interest beyond the legal rate, being against (the law), cannot be recovered; they call that a usurious way (of lending); (the lender) is (in no case) entitled to (more than) five in the hundred.
context_note: Interest is lawful in the dharmashastra but capped: beyond the legal rate lies usury, unrecoverable at law. Regulation, not prohibition, is the Hindu legal mode here.

text: To a man thinking about objects of sense, attachment to them is generated; from attachment springs desire; from desire anger is produced; from anger results want of discrimination; from want of discrimination, confusion of the memory; from confusion of the memory, loss of reason; and in consequence of loss of reason he is utterly ruined.
context_note: The Gita's causal chain from attachment to ruin, with anger as its middle link — anger is analyzed as a cognitive failure that destroys judgment, not merely a feeling.

text: This is the threefold gate of hell, destructive of the self — desire, anger and avarice; therefore one should abandon this triad.
context_note: Desire, anger, and greed as the three gates of hell: the compact Gita text cited against all three vices at once.

text: The teacher (acarya) is ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (upadhyaya), the father a hundred times more than the teacher, but the mother a thousand times more than the father.
context_note: Manu's ladder of veneration culminates in the mother; alongside verses on the unrepayable debt to parents it grounds filial duty in gratitude for existence itself.

text: That trouble (and pain) which the parents undergo on the birth of (their) children, cannot be compensated even in a hundred years.
context_note: The debt to parents is declared uncompensable in principle — the strongest possible framing of filial obligation.

text: Grass, room (for resting), water, and fourthly a kind word; these (things) never fail in the houses of good men.
context_note: Even the poorest household owes the guest these four; the guest (atithi) arrives with a claim, and turning him away unfed transfers his merit from host to guest.

text: 'Let mutual fidelity continue until death,' this may be considered as the summary of the highest law for husband and wife.
context_note: Manu's own summary of marriage law: fidelity until death, stated as mutual — the sacramental view of the bond in one sentence.

text: If the husband went abroad for some sacred duty, (she) must wait for him eight years, if (he went) to (acquire) learning or fame six (years), if (he went) for pleasure three years.
context_note: The waiting-period rules acknowledge that abandonment strains the bond; with the Arthashastra's mutual-enmity release, they show classical law grappling with marriages that fail in fact.

text: That devotee of mine, who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, who is free from egoism, and from (the idea that this or that is) mine, to whom happiness and misery are alike, who is forgiving, contented, constantly devoted, self-restrained, and firm in his determinations, and whose mind and understanding are devoted to me, he is dear to me.
context_note: The portrait of the beloved devotee: contentment, non-hatred, and freedom from 'mine' — the positive character against which envy is measured.

text: Valour, glory, courage, dexterity, not slinking away from battle, gifts, exercise of lordly power, these are the natural duties of a Kshatriya, born of (his) own nature.
context_note: Courage as svadharma: for the warrior it is constitutive duty, not optional heroism — indexed, like all Gita ethics, to station and situation.

text: Your business is with action alone; not by any means with fruit. Let not the fruit of action be your motive (to action). Let not your attachment be (fixed) on inaction.
context_note: The karma-yoga axiom: act from duty, unattached to outcome — the Gita's answer to both paralysis and ambition, and the inner form of its courage.

text: Killing a Brahmana, drinking (the spirituous liquor called) Sura, stealing (the gold of a Brahmana), adultery with a Guru's wife, and associating with such (offenders), they declare (to be) mortal sins (mahapataka).
context_note: Sura-drinking ranks among the five mortal sins for the twice-born; abstention from intoxicants belongs to ritual purity and self-command in the dharma literature.
